newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria fuel crisis caused by greed, watchdog says.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria fuel crisis caused by greed, watchdog says.

text.p: Greed and corruption are largely responsible for an acute shortage of fuel crippling Africa's oil-producing giant Nigeria, the head of an economic watchdog said on Wednesday.

"People are benefiting from the crisis. Petroleum importers are trying to ensure that more imports are necessary and refineries are making products for export when they should be producing petrol," said Sam Aluko, chairman of the National Economic Intelligence Committee.
Aluko told Reuters by telephone from his home in southwestern Akure that details of what his committee uncovered had been passed to military ruler General Sani Abacha who would soon take action.

Abacha's government ordered a halt in fuel imports last September but has been forced to resume them to end a petrol shortage that has gone into a third week and brought much of Nigeria to a standstill.
"Importers make huge profits when they bring in ships, and by helping to engineer the crisis they make sure that imports remain necessary," Aluko said.
The irony of fuel shortages in Africa's biggest oil producer has not been lost on the local press, which decried it as a national shame.
State radio on Tuesday said Abacha summoned officials of state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) and the ministries of finance and petroleum to explain the shortage.

Long queues have become commonplace at any pump station selling fuel and a black market is booming, with a 50-litre (10-gallon) can of petrol selling for as much 4,000 naira ($47) -- more than seven times the normal price.

Nigeria produces about two million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil. Of this, 250,000 bpd is allocated to four refineries, which have a combined output capacity to process 445,000 bpd but operate well below that.
"The refineries need more money to be able to ensure that they can operate at capacity," said Aluko.

"But even from their reduced capacity there are refineries producing other products for export, such as naptha, which some people are using to make money abroad rather than producing the petrol that Nigeria needs."

Last year, Nigeria spent $600 million on imports. Finance minister Anthony Ani argued this was uneconomic and this year voted $230 million to put the pipeline network and local refineries in shape so they could produce enough to export.
"The ultimate solution is to deregulate the petroleum industry. If that is done the refineries will run profitably and there will be no fuel shortage," said one NNPC official.

But Aluko said: "There is no need for outright privatisation of the refineries. That is what the private sector wants so that it can plunder Nigeria's assets. All that is required is sufficient monitoring of where the money goes."
